stories.title: Africa: Africa's Non-Communicable Diseases Burden Continues to Rise, Latest Study Finds
stories.summary: Africa's Non-Communicable Diseases Burden Continues to Rise, Latest Study Finds 5 October 2026 Content from a Premium Partner Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Addis Ababa) A 2026 Lancet Global Health analysis using Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2023 data finds that non-communicable diseases (NCDs) are accounting for a growing share of Africa's health burden. In 2023, NCDs resulted in an estimated 263 million disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), with one DALY representing one year of healthy life lost. NCDs caused an estimated 2.33 billion cases and 4.70 million deaths. The leading causes of NCD deaths in 2023 were, Ischaemic heart disease - 801,000 deaths, stroke - 700,000, chronic kidney disease - 293,000, hypertensive heart disease - 246,000 and diabetes - 245,000. The three largest contributors to NCD deaths were high systolic blood pressure - 26.2% dietary risks - 14.7%, air pollution - 14.2%.

stories.summary: Embassy Issues Ebola Alert As Kenya Traces 28 Contacts Gaitano Pessa/Daily Nation Travelers being screened for the Ebola virus at the Kenyan border (file photo) 7 October 2026 Capital FM (Nairobi) By Irene Mwangi Nairobi — The United States Embassy in Nairobi has issued a health alert following Kenya's confirmation of its first imported case of Bundibugyo virus disease, urging people at risk of exposure to seek medical guidance if they develop symptoms associated with Ebola. The alert came as Kenyan health authorities stepped up contact tracing after a Kenyan citizen who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) travelled by road to Uganda before flying to Nairobi on October 3 aboard Jambojet flight JM8523. "The Government of Kenya reported a case of Bundibugyo virus disease ('Ebola') on October 6. Health officials are conducting contact tracing of the patient," the US Embassy said in its alert issued on Tuesday. According to the Ministry of Health information cited by the embassy, the traveller crossed from the DRC into Uganda by land before taking the Jambojet flight to Jomo Kenyatta International Airport (JKIA). stories.title: Zimbabwe: Mnangagwa Declares State of Disaster As 8,500 Homes Lose Roofs in Masvingo Hailstorm
stories.summary: Zimbabwe: Mnangagwa Declares State of Disaster As 8,500 Homes Lose Roofs in Masvingo Hailstorm Rohrspatz/Pixabay Hailstorm 7 October 2026 New Zimbabwe (London) PRESIDENT Emmerson Mnangagwa has declared a State of Disaster following a severe hailstorm that hit Masvingo on Monday, leaving thousands of homes and infrastructure damaged. The hailstorm caused extensive destruction across residential areas, public utilities, education and health institutions, as well as commercial establishments. Preliminary assessments indicate that about 8,500 households had their roofs completely blown off, while 90% of the 17,000 households assessed had shattered windowpanes, leaving families exposed at the start of the rainy season. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Several major institutions were severely affected, including Great Zimbabwe University's Mucheke Campus, Masvingo Polytechnic, Masvingo Teachers College, Maud Muzenda Training Centre, the Passport Office, Grain Marketing Board, Chiefs Hall, Veterinary Office, District Development Coordinator's Office, ZIMRE Building, Masvingo Urban VTC, Runyararo Clinic Maternity Ward, Rujeko Hall, 4.1 Brigade, Masvingo Airport and the ZEC Provincial Office. Business operations in Masvingo City were also disrupted, with major retail and hospitality outlets suffering roof damage, severe leaks and damage to assets.

Dr Jean Kaseya , Director General of Africa CDC, spoke with Kenyan authorities today and expressed his condolences to the family and loved ones of the deceased, as well as to the Government and people of Kenya. Today, a high level and multidisciplinary Africa CDC team is flying to Kenya to provide appropriate support. "I thank the Kenyan authorities for the rapid measures already put in place and reiterate Africa CDC's full support. I will personally travel to Kenya in the coming days to assess, together with the national authorities, the needs of the response and any additional support required," said Dr Kaseya. Africa CDC commends the rapid identification, isolation and testing of the patient, who had travelled by road from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to Uganda, spent a night there before flying to Kenya.

stories.title: Sudan: Sudan's Death Toll in 2025 Could Be As High As 100,000 - How We Did the Count
stories.summary: Sudan's Death Toll in 2025 Could Be As High As 100,000 - How We Did the Count Mohamed Jamal Alasmer/The New Humanitarian A community kitchen prepares food in the town of Tawila, which has become a hub for people escaping RSF attacks in El Fasher and surrounding displacement camps. 6 October 2026 The Conversation Africa (Johannesburg) analysis By Paola Vesco, Amber Deniz, David Randahl, Johan BroschÃ© and Magnus Ãberg Estimates of the number of people directly killed in Sudan's civil war vary widely, in part because counting casualties in active conflict zones is extremely difficult. In 2025, for instance, one conflict monitoring organisation reported around 19,000 direct deaths from political violence across Sudan. Other research teams put the toll at more than 70,000 . Conflict researcher Paola Vesco and her team have developed a model that helps measure the uncertainty around such conflict death estimates. Their approach takes into account the tendency of conflict datasets to underestimate fatalities, and provides a more realistic range of possible death tolls.

stories.title: Congo-Kinshasa: 'Ebola Takes the People Children Depend On' - UNICEF
stories.summary: Congo-Kinshasa: 'Ebola Takes the People Children Depend On' - UNICEF Grainne Harrington/WHO A patient is carried to an Ebola treatment centre in the DR Congo. 6 October 2026 UN News Service The Ebola outbreak in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is robbing children of their loved ones - with some succumbing to the deadly disease themselves, the UN Children's Fund (UNICEF) reported on Tuesday. The update comes as neighbouring Kenya confirmed its first case and death from the disease, believed to have come from DRC. " Ebola takes the people children depend on and unravels their lives ," said Halimatou Amadou, UNICEF Chief of Communication in the DRC, speaking to journalists in Geneva. "The parents fall ill, a child may be exposed, the parent is taken for treatment or dies. At the very moment a child most needs someone, fear and stigma can keep relatives and neighbours away." Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Nearly 2,000 children affected More than 1,900 boys and girls have either lost one or both parents, or their caregivers, since the outbreak was declared in May, or have been separated from them. Most of these children, 1,581, are in North Kivu province, the epicentre of the crisis. A further 322 are in neighbouring North Kivu province. "And these are the children we know about because these figures cover only the area where UNICEF works with social affairs teams in the affected provinces," she said.

stories.summary: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 7, 2026 AllAfrica AllAfrica logo 7 October 2026 allAfrica.com press review By Melody Chironda Mali Army Retakes Kidal With Russian Support Mali's army, backed by Russian paramilitary forces, has retaken the northern town of Kidal after Tuareg separatists announced a "strategic and controlled withdrawal" from the area. The Azawad Liberation Front said its forces withdrew without direct fighting, attributing the move to what it described as the disproportionate use of air power by Russia's Africa Corps. Kidal has long been a stronghold of Tuareg separatists seeking an independent state in northern Mali. It was previously seized by the separatists and an al-Qaeda-linked group. The recapture is being viewed as a symbolic victory for Mali's military government, which has increasingly turned to Russia for military support after distancing itself from France.

Cette perte de Kidal avait à l'époque constitué un véritable camouflet pour les forces armées maliennes, survenue lors d'attaques d'ampleur et coordonnées contre des positions de la junte et de l'armée dans plusieurs villes, y compris aux abords de Bamako. Depuis 2012, le Mali fait face à une profonde crise sécuritaire, nourrie notamment par les violences de groupes jihadistes, de leurs alliés du FLA et de groupes criminels communautaires.

stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5NpxV Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed was on Monday sworn in for a new five-year mandate Image: Ethiopian PM Office Advertisement Amid escalating conflict in Ethiopia's northernmost Tigray region , Abiy Ahmed has been sworn in for another term as Prime Minister of Ethiopia . Shortly after the ceremony on Monday afternoon, Abiy reiterated his will to work toward giving the landlocked country direct access to the Red Sea . "Based on the principle of give and take, we will work diligently to ensure that Ethiopia has an outlet to the sea," Abiy said, a remark that risks exacerbating tensions with neighboring Eritrea . The two countries have been at odds over Ethiopia's desire to control Eritrea's port of Assab . DW correspondent Solomon Muchie, who followed the swearing-in ceremony in Addis Ababa, said despite the renewed mandate, Abiy faces challenging times ahead. "The new term gives Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed stronger political authority," Solomon said. "But the country's complex internal and regional challenges could make it difficult to translate the authority into lasting stability." Sunday's meeting in Cairo of countries that opposed Ethiopia was a case in point, Munchie said. "The leaders of Egypt , Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan discussed regional issues, but Ethiopia was excluded from this meeting, so this is also what Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government will face in his tenure in the coming years." Ethiopia still eyeing Eritrea's port of Assab For analyst Abdurahman Sayed, who leads the London-based Horn of Africa Center for Regional Integration, Eritrea now faces an imminent threat of entering the war in Tigray . This comes after a three-year Ethiopian campaign to gain control of the port of Assab. "Eritrea has legitimate concern of Ethiopia's intentions to occupy [the country] if it can, and then if not, then at least take the port of Assab, which is a very important port, not only for commercial purposes but also strategically," Sayed said. "It oversees the Bab el Mandeb [Strait] , which is the southern entrance to the Red Sea.

stories.title: ‘There’s always been a belittling of African women’: honouring history’s invisible heroines
stories.summary: As demand for it drove the transatlantic slave trade, sugar symbolises the sacrifice of people for goods. Photograph: Pamela Tulizo Congolese photographer Pamela Tulizo uses costume and vivid scenery to celebrate women’s strength and give a new perspective on slavery By Sarah Johnson P amela Tulizo’s latest series of photographs started with a question. “I asked myself, why are women in my community in particular, and African women in general, so strong?” says Tulizo, an artist and photographer from the Democratic Republic of the Congo . “Where does this strength come from?” Growing up in Goma in eastern DRC, Tulizo was informed and inspired by the women she was surrounded by, including her mother, her sisters, her mother’s friends and her neighbours. Years later, when she began to look into the role of women throughout African history, she says: “I realised that perhaps women have been forced to be strong since the dawn of time, forced by circumstance to build that resilience.” View image in fullscreen Women are placed at the centre of the series of 23 staged photographs Her research brought her to slavery, the “cruellest period in human history”, which is often just associated with the men who were forced across oceans to form workforces abroad. Women, she noticed, were largely invisible, their stories untold. With that in mind, Tulizo placed women at the centre of her series of 23 staged photographs called Mababu (“ancestors” in Swahili).

La hausse des prix, notamment des fruits et des légumes, s’explique en partie par une production agricole limitée à cause des feux de forêt durant l’été , atteignant des niveaux historiquement hauts.

stories.title: Côte d’Ivoire: une partie de l'opposition propose une nouvelle Commission électorale après sa dissolution
stories.summary: Côte d’Ivoire: une partie de l'opposition propose une nouvelle Commission électorale après sa dissolution En Côte d’Ivoire, plusieurs partis d’opposition se sont accordés sur des propositions communes concernant la future institution chargée d'organiser les scrutins, après la dissolution en mai dernier de la Commission électorale indépendante (CEI). Le document, élaboré après plusieurs semaines de concertation, a été remis lundi 5 octobre au ministère de l’Intérieur. Mais les deux principaux partis d’opposition étaient quant à eux absents. Publié le : 06/10/2026 - 00:24 Modifié le : 06/10/2026 - 00:24 3 min Temps de lecture Une entrée du siège de la Commission électorale indépendante (CEI) à Abidjan, en octobre 2025 © RFI Par : RFI Publicité Lire la suite Avec notre correspondante à Abidjan, Fanny Noaro-Kabré En Côte d'Ivoire , le PPA-CI de Laurent Gbagbo , la CAP-CI, qui comprend notamment le FPI de Pascal Affi N’Guessan, l’ADCI d’Assalé Tiémoko et la plateforme HCE emmenée par l’ancienne première dame Simone Ehivet ont participé aux discussions sur les contours du futur organe électoral. Depuis l’annonce, en mai dernier, de la dissolution de la Commission électorale indépendante , les partis de l’opposition, très critiques à l’égard de l’ancienne CEI, qu’ils accusaient notamment de partialité, se concertaient pour élaborer une feuille de route commune.

stories.title: De Casablanca à Abidjan, comment les deux places boursières séduisent les investisseurs étrangers
stories.summary: De Casablanca à Abidjan, comment les deux places boursières séduisent les investisseurs étrangers Les deux places boursières attirent de plus en plus de capitaux venus de l’extérieur. Parmi leurs avantages comparatifs, la stabilité monétaire, des secteurs porteurs et des liquidités en hausse. stories.title: Bombs preventing rescue of kidnapped youths, Nigerian police say
stories.summary: Image caption, Omotosho Adewale, the father of one of those abducted, says he has had no peace and has not eaten for three days By Makuochi Okafor BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Lagos Published 5 October 2026 Nigerian police say they have located a camp where 19 national youth service recruits are being held by gunmen but cannot move in as they believe the place is mined with explosives. Police Commissioner Audu Bosso said drones helped locate the camp where the prospective National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) members were taken after being abducted last week in the south-eastern Imo state. The exact location of the camp has not been disclosed and police have not identified those responsible for the kidnapping. Omotosho Adewale, whose child is among those abducted, told the BBC that the kidnappers had demanded a ransom of 50m naira ($37,680; Â£28,440), which he could not afford. "There's no peace of mind. I've not eaten in three days," he said in between tears.

stories.title: Guardian readers fund life-changing surgery for Somali boy injured in US airstrike
stories.summary: Abdiqadir Salah and his mother, Marian Haji Abdi Guled. ‘I didn’t know people like this existed,’ she says of the people who raised the money for her son’s surgery. Photograph: Mohamed Gabobe View image in fullscreen Abdiqadir Salah and his mother, Marian Haji Abdi Guled. ‘I didn’t know people like this existed,’ she says of the people who raised the money for her son’s surgery. Photograph: Mohamed Gabobe Guardian readers fund life-changing surgery for Somali boy injured in US airstrike After Guardian investigation uncovered drone strike that killed 12 civilians and injured many more, seven-year-old Abdiqadir Salah underwent vital operation in Mogadishu On the rickshaw ride to the hospital, Marian Haji Abdi Guled felt a mixture of joy and apprehension: the day they had been waiting for had finally arrived. Almost a year earlier, her then seven-year-old son, Abdiqadir Salah, had been seriously injured, alongside his two siblings, in what a Guardian investigation found was a US drone strike on the village of Jamaame in Somalia that killed at least 12 civilians, including eight children. Abdiqadir’s small body had been impaled by shrapnel in the attack, and several chunks remained embedded in his back.

stories.title: Ethiopian rebel forces withdraw from Tigray regional capital
stories.summary: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, A pro-government soldier standing guard on a street in Ethiopia's Tigray region on Sunday By Teklemariam Bekit ,Â editor, BBC Tigrinya, Â and Â Jack Burgess Published 4 October 2026 Updated 5 October 2026 Rebel forces in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region have said they have temporarily withdrawn from the regional capital, Mekelle, as fighting with the national army moves towards the city. The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which has been running the region, said it decised to leave because of concerns about risks to civilians. Two Mekelle residents told the BBC that pro-government forces now control the city and TPLF fighters have abandoned it. One resident also said mobile phone services had been restored. Fighting has erupted in recent weeks between the TPLF and allied groups and government forces in parts of the northern regions of Tigray, Afar and Amhara.

stories.title: Skull fractures suggest servants of Egypt’s ancient kings were sacrificed
stories.summary: A fresco depicting a funeral procession in ancient Egypt. Photograph: DEA/F Guenet/De Agostini/Getty Images View image in fullscreen A fresco depicting a funeral procession in ancient Egypt. Photograph: DEA/F Guenet/De Agostini/Getty Images Skull fractures suggest servants of Egypt’s ancient kings were sacrificed Study of remains taken from royal cemetery at Umm el-Qa’ab appears to confirm early Egyptologist’s theory Court officials and craftspeople serving early Egyptian kings may have been sacrificed when their ruler died, according to research that found fractures in several ancient skulls. The royal cemetery of Umm el-Qa’ab near Abydos features the tombs and enclosures of the First Dynasty rulers of Egypt, and dates as far back as 3,000BC. Not only royalty were buried at the site: surrounding these structures are graves thought to belong to people associated with the royal households – including ladies, seal-bearers, inspectors and artisans.

stories.title: Anthropic report: Is Russia using AI for disinformation in the Central African Republic and elsewhere across Africa?
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5NTaF The Claude app was allegedly misused by Russian agents Image: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/picture alliance Advertisement In Bangui, the capital of the Central African Republic , Russian agents are said to have deliberately used the AI assistant Claude to promote pro-Russian influence. A report titled " Detecting and Countering Misuse of AI ," published by US-based company Anthropic in September, detailed how opposition politicians were monitored, propaganda content was created and disinformation campaigns were supported. The report claimed that Claude was used primarily to produce content broadcast by Radio Lengo Songo, a radio station that, according to the international investigative collective All Eyes on Wagner, is funded by Russia. The collective, made up of journalists, academics and experts, investigates the activities of the Russian mercenary Wagner Group and its successor structures, such as the Africa Corps, around the world. Pro-Russian propaganda, surveillance of the opposition The Anthropic report said the content was pro-Russian and portrayed the Central African government and the Africa Corps mercenaries in a positive light, while taking a critical stance on France and the opposition.

stories.title: Niger : disparu depuis août, le journaliste Moussa Kaka est « détenu » par les autorités
stories.summary: Niger : disparu depuis août, le journaliste Moussa Kaka est « détenu » par les autorités La junte menée par Abdourahamane Tiani reprocherait au directeur de la chaîne RTS, et ancien correspondant de RFI, d’avoir « commis une infraction », sans préciser laquelle, et a annoncé qu’il devrait « répondre devant les juridictions ». Le journaliste nigérian Moussa Kaka, ancien correspondant de RFI et de RSF, et directeur de Radio-Télévision Saraounia, le 12 février 2005. © SEYLLOU DIALLO / AFP Par Jeune Afrique Publié aujourd'hui à 10h29 Lecture : 2 minutes. Le Niger est dirigé depuis 2023 par un régime militaire régulièrement accusé par des ONG d’atteintes à la liberté de la presse . Le sort de Moussa Kaka, 66 ans et directeur d’une télévision privée, suscitait de nombreuses inquiétudes depuis sa disparition le 31 août, quelques jours après une mutinerie qui avait secoué Niamey et que le régime militaire avait finalement déjouée avec l’aide déterminante de son allié russe.

stories.title: Howard W. French, écrivain : « L’Afrique doit trouver ses propres moyens d’élaborer des projets nationaux et continentaux, la solution ne viendra pas d’ailleurs »
stories.summary: Le journaliste et auteur consacre son dernier ouvrage à Kwame Nkrumah, héraut du panafricanisme et père de l’indépendance du Ghana, en 1957. French explique, dans un entretien au « Monde », que la montée en puissance de l’Afrique sur la scène internationale dépend notamment de l’union de ses Etats.

stories.title: Knox Chitiyo obituary
stories.summary: Knox Chitiyo left Zimbabwe in 2005 to live in the UK, where he was head of the Royal United Services Institute’s Africa programme View image in fullscreen Knox Chitiyo left Zimbabwe in 2005 to live in the UK, where he was head of the Royal United Services Institute’s Africa programme Obituary Knox Chitiyo obituary My friend and former colleague Knox Chitiyo, who has died aged 65 of bowel cancer, was a Zimbabwean academic and later an important voice in Britain on his homeland and its future. He was regularly consulted by diplomats, business people, journalists, academics and activists. From 1992 to 2003 he was a senior lecturer in war studies and military history at the University of Zimbabwe, where he co-founded the Centre for Defence Studies, serving as its deputy director. He also taught on the joint command and staff course at Zimbabwe’s National Army Staff College and at the Gweru Military Academy, helping shape the strategic thinking of a generation of officers. As intellectual space in Zimbabwe tightened under Robert Mugabe , Knox moved to the UK in 2005.

stories.title: Egyptian journalist faces terrorism charges after entire newsroom detained
stories.summary: Clockwise from top left: Mohamed Ashraf, Omar Helal, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Adel, Mohamed Mahmoud and Abdallah Qadri. Photograph: Matsadaash/AP View image in fullscreen Clockwise from top left: Mohamed Ashraf, Omar Helal, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Adel, Mohamed Mahmoud and Abdallah Qadri. Photograph: Matsadaash/AP Egyptian journalist faces terrorism charges after entire newsroom detained Calls for release of six Matsadaash staff after one is charged, while whereabouts of other five remain unknown An Egyptian journalist has been charged with joining a terrorist group, days after an entire newsroom was detained in what rights groups have said is a crackdown on press freedoms. Last week, authorities arrested six journalists from the independent fact-checking and investigative platform Matsadaash – literally meaning “don’t believe” – accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and publishing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood . The outlet’s six journalists, Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal, were arrested by security forces over the course of two days.

stories.title: Why pastors may not be seen - or heard - preaching on Ghana's buses for much longer
stories.summary: Figure caption, Boateng Bismark James has been preaching on buses leaving Neoplan station since 2023 By Thomas Naadi BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Accra Published 4 October 2026 Before the morning rush begins, the sound of praise and worship fills the Neoplan bus station in Ghana's capital, Accra, as a group of Christians gather to prepare to evangelise on vehicles taking travellers across the country. Amid drumming and dancing, Boateng Bismark James leads 13 worshippers, nine men and four women, in prayer for drivers and passengers travelling to destinations across Ghana. Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread. On long-distance buses, pastors can often be seen - and heard - preaching the gospel. Sometimes they stand in the stairwell next to the driver, at others they walk up and down the aisle reading from the Bible and calling on sinners to repent at the tops of their voices.

stories.title: Morocco's first female head of government: Symbol or real reform?
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5NfFo Mansouri has been nicknamed the "pasha's daughter" because she comes from a prominent Marrakesh family and her father was formerly a pasha or municipal governor Image: Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP Advertisement After the announcement that Morocco would appoint its first female head of government – Marrakech mayor Fatima Zahra Mansouri – citizens interviewed by local television reporters were mostly enthusiastic. "It would be great if we had a female prime minister for a change. She'd lift our spirits a bit," one woman said. "Why don't we give women a chance? We've never had one [a female head of government] before," said another. "May God bless her and help her stay on a straight path." "Regardless of who takes on the role, it should be a change for the better in Morocco," a man added. Morocco's King Mohammed VI chose Fatima Zahra Mansouri to be the country's first female prime minister following September's parliamentary elections Image: Mosa'ab Elshamy/AP Photo/picture alliance But there were also naysayers. Some locals questioned how she would take part in official events where tradition and protocol dictate that only men attend. "People are saying that a nation cannot succeed if a woman is in charge, even if she's only half in charge," one man told a television reporter, referring to the fact that Morocco's King Mohammed VI has the final say in national politics.

stories.title: The South African men trying to end violence against women: 'Every man needs to play a part'
stories.summary: Image source, Christian Parkinson/ BBC Image caption, Kgomotso Mathekga says a lack of male role models is fuelling violence against women in his neighbourhood By Christian Parkinson Reporting from Johannesburg Published 3 October 2026 "I witness men hitting women all the time," says Kgomotso Mathekga, 30. "Especially when they are both drunk." "I once had an argument with my girlfriend," he admits, "and I grabbed and slapped her." Mathekga is speaking frankly during a gathering of men aimed at helping reduce the high levels of violence against women in South Africa. The meeting is held in a narrow street in a Johannesburg informal settlement known as Organic Market. It is a maze of corrugated metal shacks and unpaved roads, close to Alexandra township. "Now I feel pain," Mathekga continues. "We broke up and I no longer see my child. I feel like I've contributed to the problems in South Africa, instead of being the gentleman that I know I am." At a nearby tavern, a group of men have pulled their chairs into a circle in the dust. At the centre stands Itumeleng Stephen Tamaga, known locally as Bra Steve.

stories.title: John Iliffe obituary
stories.summary: John Iliffe’s work was regarded internationally as the model of what engaged research should be. Photograph: Nordin Ćatić/St John's College, Cambridge View image in fullscreen John Iliffe’s work was regarded internationally as the model of what engaged research should be. Photograph: Nordin Ćatić/St John's College, Cambridge Obituary John Iliffe obituary Pioneering historian who transformed the study of Africa by seeking out the testimonies of Africans When John Iliffe, who has died aged 87, wrote his book The African Poor: A History (1987), the continent was readily dismissed by many academics as a home of problems and poverty, with no intellectual depth. But Iliffe acknowledged no such limitations, and it came as no surprise that it won the African Studies Association’s best book prize, then known as the Herskovits prize. In Iliffe’s view, people who are excluded from production, productive resources and land in otherwise land-rich economies are not just statistics who merely suffer.

stories.summary: Publicité L'armée éthiopienne patrouille dans Mekele, ses rivaux inquiets se réunissent en Égypte Afrique L'armée fédérale éthiopienne et une milice tigréenne alliée contrôlent dimanche Mekele, capitale de l'État régional du Tigré. stories.title: Trump is disappearing refugees into the hands of torturers – and rewarding them handsomely | Tutu Alicante and Uzra Zeya
stories.summary: ‘Adam and everyone held at Hotel Bamy should be released and given the chance to have their asylum claims heard in a country capable of hearing them.’ Photograph: Monika Pronczuk/AP View image in fullscreen ‘Adam and everyone held at Hotel Bamy should be released and given the chance to have their asylum claims heard in a country capable of hearing them.’ Photograph: Monika Pronczuk/AP Trump is disappearing refugees into the hands of torturers – and rewarding them handsomely Tutu Alicante and Uzra Zeya Refugees from third countries are being sent to Equatorial Guinea, where they are often sent back to the very countries they fled F or nearly a year, the Hotel Bamy in Malabo, Equatorial Guinea , has been Adam’s prison. He is confined alone to a hotel room, under constant watch by the security officers and soldiers of a notoriously oppressive regime who control his movements. Not long ago, they barged into his room, handcuffed and beat him, and warned him not to tell anyone. There is no cell to point to, no charges or formal sentence, and nothing on paper to document his plight. Adam, 26, has chosen not to share his real name or even his country of origin out of fear for his safety.

stories.title: How fresh fighting in Tigray could spark wider conflict in Ethiopia
stories.summary: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Tigrayan forces have been patrolling the streets of Tigray's capital, Mekelle, this week By Lucy Fleming Â and Â BBC Africa Published 26 September 2026 Updated 2 October 2026 Fighting has erupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray between regional forces and the national army. Tigray residents, who have been trying to recover from a brutal two-year war that ended in 2022, fear a return to full-scale conflict. There are reports of panic buying - and now internet and call services have been disrupted. This means people cannot get access to their money via digital apps in what has become a largely cashless society after ATMs stopped working several months ago. Why has fighting broken out now?

stories.title: Row erupts over Cairo mural depicting Tutankhamun and Nefertiti with dark skin
stories.summary: The mural in Tahrir Square was designed by a volunteer youth group, Rasmet Basma, with the help of AI. Photograph: Rasmet Basma View image in fullscreen The mural in Tahrir Square was designed by a volunteer youth group, Rasmet Basma, with the help of AI. Photograph: Rasmet Basma Row erupts over Cairo mural depicting Tutankhamun and Nefertiti with dark skin Artwork created in Tahrir Square for Chinese president’s state visit to Egypt is painted over amid allegations it revived Afrocentric claims about pharaohs’ origins On the eve of the Chinese president Xi Jinping’s state visit to Cairo last month, the city authorities were busy removing a 66-metre-long mural from the esteemed guest’s line of sight. Depicting the Pharaoh Tutankhamun and Queen Nefertiti, the painting was among 40 murals commissioned to beautify the city for Xi’s arrival and was painted by a group of young volunteers, Rasmet Basma, in Tahrir Square. But it drew a furious reaction for depicting the two historical figures with dark skin – angering those Egyptians who saw it as reviving Afrocentric claims about the 14th-century BCE pharaoh’s origins.

stories.title: One green shoot at a time: the women restoring mangrove forests in the oil-ravaged Niger delta
stories.summary: Martha Agbani, centre, with some of the women planters she has trained in mangrove restoration techniques in the Niger delta, an area devastated by five decades of oil pollution. Photograph: Valentine Benjamin View image in fullscreen Martha Agbani, centre, with some of the women planters she has trained in mangrove restoration techniques in the Niger delta, an area devastated by five decades of oil pollution. Photograph: Valentine Benjamin One green shoot at a time: the women restoring mangrove forests in the oil-ravaged Niger delta In a region of Nigeria blighted by decades of pollution, Martha Agbani and her team are not just replanting trees but regaining ownership of their lost lands and livelihoods A toxic landscape was familiar to Martha Agbani when she was growing up – the smell of crude oil in the air, rivers running black and trees dying on the banks. In Ogoniland, in Nigeria’s oil-exploited Niger delta, Agbani saw the spills rot away the mangrove forests and destroy the livelihoods of communities around her. Now, she is training women to plant them back – one fragile green shoot at a time.

stories.title: Making politics 'fun, trendy, sexy': How Gen Z could shape Kenya's next election
stories.summary: Image source, Reuters By Barbara Plett Usher Africa correspondent ,Â Reporting from Nairobi, Kangema & Meru Published 2 October 2026 Ademba Allans is making it "cool" to vote in Kenya. stories.title: Alan Ferguson obituary
stories.summary: Alan Ferguson, a fluent speaker of Swahili, worked for aid agencies in Kenya on family planning and public health View image in fullscreen Alan Ferguson, a fluent speaker of Swahili, worked for aid agencies in Kenya on family planning and public health Obituary Alan Ferguson obituary My brother, Alan Ferguson, who has died aged 79, was a Scotsman who began his working life as a geography lecturer at Nairobi University in Kenya , before working with aid agencies in that country. Alan joined the university in 1972, but left after a couple of years to teach in Britain at Cambridge University, and then in the US at NorthEastern University in Chicago. However, Kenya had got a hold on him, and he returned to work there, first for Amref , a Dutch organisation, and then GTZ, a German body, mainly in family planning and public health. Eventually he went freelance, helping various aid agencies with their work in Kenya, until a serious accident incapacitated him, forcing him to retire to Scotland. Born in Glasgow , Alan was the son of Bill, an analytical chemist, and Jessie (nee Moncrieff), a shorthand typist.

stories.title: ‘They raped our country’: documentary follows Kenyans’ fight for restitution over stolen land
stories.summary: Much of the land taken during the colonial era has remained with the political elite and foreign companies occupying huge tea plantations. Photograph: Andrew H Brown View image in fullscreen Much of the land taken during the colonial era has remained with the political elite and foreign companies occupying huge tea plantations. Photograph: Andrew H Brown ‘They raped our country’: documentary follows Kenyans’ fight for restitution over stolen land Multinational tea companies still occupy ancestral highlands of communities displaced during British colonial era F or British colonialists, the fertile and cool uplands of central Kenya were the “White Highlands”, to be reserved exclusively for European settlers. Local communities were forced from the land, which was turned into plantations for tea and other crops. In recent decades, descendants of the displaced have fought to reclaim their ancestral land, some of which is now occupied by multinational tea companies and other large corporations.

stories.title: Trump administration diverts human rights funds to push far-right agenda abroad
stories.summary: Afrikaner refugees from South Africa hold American flags as they arrive at Dulles airport in Washington last May. Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP View image in fullscreen Afrikaner refugees from South Africa hold American flags as they arrive at Dulles airport in Washington last May. Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Trump administration diverts human rights funds to push far-right agenda abroad Support such as for white Afrikaners and anti-communism reveals how US is redefining what qualifies as human rights With hours left before the funding expires, the Trump administration is pushing to direct more than $175m of the state department’s flagship human rights fund to a slate of awards that includes a huge $40m grant for an anti-communism fund, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa, a campaign against Brazil’s supreme court and programs that would reward ideological allies in Europe who protect “western civilizational norms”. On Wednesday, the state department obligated the funds to the grantees hours before the deadline despite congressional concerns and requests not to do so, according to a source familiar with the negotiations. The state department declined to comment on questions from the Guardian specifically on whether it had obligated the funds and had “blown” holds from Congress due to concerns about the money’s use.

stories.title: Five EU states plan first deportation center in Africa for 2027
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5NX1O Prospective migrants who arrived in Greece are taken into a migration hub Image: Sofia Kleftaki/DW Advertisement Deportation centers are legally contentious, expensive and the subject of political controversy: For years, Brussels has been grappling with the issue of establishing such centers outside the EU for rejected asylum seekers. Previous attempts have failed due to legal objections, but now, a "group of five" consisting of Greece , Germany , Austria , Denmark and the Netherlands believes it has overcome these hurdles . During an interview with the Greek television channel ANT1, Greece's Minister of Migration, Thanos Plevris, stated that the first of these so-called " return hubs " is scheduled to begin operations as early as the second half of 2027 — just in time for Greece to assume the EU Council Presidency. Plevris said Greece had chosen an African country but could not reveal its name yet. Diplomatic circles and media outlets close to the EU have repeatedly cited Rwanda or Uganda , but neither country has been confirmed as the location.

stories.title: South African leader urges men to speak up on gender-based violence after series of killings
stories.summary: South Africa has been gripped with grief and fury after the discovery of 11 women’s bodies dumped across Ekurhuleni, a city adjoining Johannesburg, since 15 July. Photograph: Esa Alexander/Reuters View image in fullscreen South Africa has been gripped with grief and fury after the discovery of 11 women’s bodies dumped across Ekurhuleni, a city adjoining Johannesburg, since 15 July. Photograph: Esa Alexander/Reuters South African leader urges men to speak up on gender-based violence after series of killings President announces measures amid anger at authorities over recent murders of women South Africa’s president has called on men to take more responsibility for violence against women as he announced measures to tackle the problem, amid anger at authorities over a recent wave of murders. Cyril Ramaphosa acknowledged that not enough had been done to protect women. He said police would be reviewing unsolved murders, attempted murders and serious sexual offences against women and children, as well as producing a funded plan to reduce the forensic backlog for such cases, both within 60 days.
